title: Meet the innovators under 35 shaping climate tech
gist: Reading nine young climate-and-energy innovators as a cohort yields three signals about where climate tech is heading: AI is both the sector's biggest energy problem and one of its most useful research tools; critical-minerals extraction (lithium from brine and hardrock, with copper next) is drawing startup formation ahead of a possible shortage this decade; and decarbonization work is spreading into unglamorous corners like steel furnaces, refrigerants, bioplastics and aquaculture feed.

themes.theme: AI as both climate problem and climate tool

insights.claim: AI is described as the dominant technology story in climate innovation, notable both for its potential and for the challenges it creates.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Any climate-tech thesis that treats AI only as a demand shock or only as a tool is missing half the trade.
insights.quote: AI is the dominant technology story, both for its potential and its challenges.

insights.claim: Even after splitting an innovator cohort into four categories — biotech, climate and energy, computing and robotics, and AI — AI still features heavily in the work of many innovators outside the AI category.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: AI is behaving as general-purpose infrastructure across research domains rather than as a standalone vertical.
insights.quote: It probably won’t surprise you that AI features heavily in the work of many innovators in other categories.

insights.claim: One innovator built software that makes AI more energy-efficient by measuring the energy demands of open-source models, on the premise that the industry cannot address its energy impact without first measuring it.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Measurement tooling is the upstream bottleneck for AI energy accountability — and a defensible niche before regulation arrives.
insights.quote: By measuring the energy demands of open-source models, he hopes the industry can better understand and address the impact of AI.

insights.claim: Machine learning is being used to fill in gaps in pollution data drawn from disparate sources such as satellites and weather stations, improving pollution tracking.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Data-fusion AI turns existing, incomplete sensor networks into usable environmental monitoring without new hardware capex.
insights.quote: essentially using machine learning to fill in gaps in data from disparate sources like satellites and weather stations

insights.claim: Cities are a well-known blind spot for traditional climate models, and AI-based climate models have been developed specifically to work better at the urban scale.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Urban-resolution climate projection is where adaptation spending decisions get made, so closing that modeling gap has direct commercial pull.
insights.quote: Zhonghua Zheng developed AI climate models that work better for cities, a well-known blind spot for traditional models.

insights.claim: Shifting to new energy technologies implies a major shift in the materials needed to build them, making critical-materials sourcing a first-order constraint rather than a downstream detail.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Frames upstream extraction as the chokepoint that gates deployment of everything downstream.
insights.quote: As we begin to rely on new technologies to power our world, we’ll see a major shift in the materials we need to build them.

insights.claim: Lithium shortages could arrive as soon as this decade, and the prospect of supply crunches applies to other critical minerals as well, with copper singled out as another one to watch closely.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A near-dated supply-crunch call on lithium and copper is directly tradable against miners, battery makers and grid-storage developers.
insights.quote: We could face lithium shortages as soon as this decade, and the prospect of supply crunches applies to other critical minerals, too—copper is another one to watch closely.

insights.claim: Lithium underpins lithium-ion batteries, which are crucial not only for electric vehicles but also for large-scale energy storage on the grid, so lithium demand is exposed to two growth markets at once.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Grid storage stacks on top of EV demand, meaning lithium demand does not decelerate if EV adoption stalls.
insights.quote: The metal underpins lithium-ion batteries, which are crucial not only for electric vehicles, but also for large-scale energy storage on the grid.

insights.claim: Brine is currently the cheapest source of lithium, but extracting the metal from it can take months and harm the local environment — a cost advantage offset by time and environmental penalties.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Identifies exactly where a technology startup can capture value: speed and environmental footprint, not headline extraction cost.
insights.quote: Brine is currently the cheapest source of lithium, but the process to get the metal out can take months and harm the local environment.

insights.claim: A startup is working to extract lithium from brines quickly and efficiently, targeting the months-long timeline that makes conventional brine extraction slow.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Names a specific private company attacking the brine bottleneck, useful for tracking the direct-lithium-extraction cohort.
insights.quote: Mohammad Alkhadra is the cofounder and CEO of Lithios, a startup working to quickly and efficiently extract lithium from brines.

insights.claim: Hardrock ore is the most common source of lithium but is more expensive than brine, and a separate startup is working specifically on extracting lithium from hardrock ore.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Two distinct startup approaches map to the two distinct lithium resource bases — cost-reduction on hardrock versus speed on brine.
insights.quote: Benjamin Mowbray cofounded and serves as CTO for Rock Zero, which is working to extract lithium from hardrock ore.

insights.claim: Addressing climate change will require overhauling all corners of society, sometimes in surprising ways, because beyond the primary sources of climate pollution lie seemingly infinite less obvious problems.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: The investable surface area of climate tech is far wider than grid and transport, which is where most capital currently concentrates.
insights.quote: Addressing climate change will require overhauling all corners of our society, sometimes in surprising ways.

insights.claim: Heavy industry including steel production makes up about 7% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A single hard-to-abate sector at 7% of global emissions justifies a dedicated technology and capital track.
insights.quote: Heavy industry, including steel production, is a major one, making up about 7% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

insights.claim: Cleaner, cheaper steel is being pursued via a new kind of furnace that simplifies the chemical process required to produce the metal — pitching cost reduction and emissions reduction together rather than as a trade-off.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Green steel that is also cheaper removes the green-premium objection that has stalled adoption.
insights.quote: Laureen Meroueh is making cleaner, cheaper steel using a new kind of furnace that simplifies the chemical process required to produce the metal.

insights.claim: Because plastics are generally made with fossil fuels, alternatives are needed, and one approach makes a bioplastic replacement for fossil-derived packaging out of an invasive weed.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Invasive-species feedstock converts a negative-cost waste stream into raw material, a pattern worth screening for across materials startups.
insights.quote: Joseph Nguthiru is making a bioplastic replacement for fossil-derived packaging that uses an invasive weed.

insights.claim: Food waste is being converted into fish food for aquaculture, another example of using already-available materials in a creative way.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Feed inputs are an overlooked emissions and cost lever in aquaculture supply chains.
insights.quote: Also using available materials in a creative way, Diana Orembe is making fish food for aquaculture with food waste.

insights.claim: Refrigerants are often incredibly powerful greenhouse gases, and solid refrigerants under development could eliminate worries about leakage while a device using them could cut energy consumption by 20% versus conventional technology.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A 20% efficiency gain plus elimination of leakage risk attacks both the direct and indirect emissions of cooling at once.
insights.quote: A device using these materials could reduce energy consumption by 20% compared to conventional technology.

themes.theme: Reading a cohort as a signal

insights.claim: Treating a year's cohort of young climate and energy innovators as a group — rather than as individual profiles — is proposed as a method for inferring where climate tech currently stands and where it is heading.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Cohort composition is a leading indicator of where research talent — and therefore the next wave of startups — is allocating itself.
insights.quote: Taken together, these innovators and their work can tell us something about where climate tech is at this moment—and where it’s heading.

insights.claim: The climate and energy category of the newest under-35 list includes nine individuals drawn from all over the world, out of a full slate of 35 innovators.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Roughly a quarter of the cohort sitting in climate and energy indicates the field still commands a substantial share of young research talent.
insights.quote: the final slate includes nine individuals from all over the world in the climate and energy category
